events.content: Stage 'positions_and_core_issues' begins
Absent active concessions, positions harden and a trilateral package drifts further away.
With the U.S.-Mexico bilateral already in place, Canada is pressured to concede to join the package.
Weak labor enforcement hardens domestic opposition.

Discussion so far:
  ustr: Here's what we're doing: Mexico's on board with 75% regional value content and a labor-value-content floor. Canada either takes the same package or we move forward bilaterally with Mexico and renegotiate with you separately later. What's it gonna be?
  canada_min: We're not signing a package we didn't shape, and we're not accepting auto rules that weren't negotiated trilaterally. 75% RVC with a labor floor—fine, let's talk specifics—but Chapter 19 and supply management are off the table, and any sunset clause harder than a review mechanism costs us the deal. What's Mexico actually getting on labor enforcement?
  canada_min: You said labor-value-content floor—but what does enforcement actually look like? Inspections? Fines? Independent monitors? Because if it's just a checkbox, Mexico's deal doesn't hold up politically for me at home, and neither does ours. That's the real trilateral problem you've got.
  ustr: The Mexico deal locks in independent labor inspections at the factory level with real fines—up to 20% tariff suspension if violations aren't corrected within 60 days. That's enforceable, and you're getting the same mechanism. Now: are you willing to match the 75% RVC and labor floor, or do we finalize this bilaterally?
  mexico_neg: Look, Canada—the labor-enforcement floor is real: independent inspections, 20% tariff hit if you don't fix violations in 60 days. That's what we've locked in with the U.S., and it's the same for all three of us. Chapter 19 and dairy are separate conversations; don't let those block the auto package. Sign the trilateral on these terms and we move forward together.
  us_congress: USTR, here's my read: labor enforcement is solid enough for Congress. But if Chapter 19 and dairy are blocking a trilateral auto signature, we're stuck. Can you move the auto deal to signature *separately* and negotiate those chapters in parallel? Because my members need to see forward motion—a package that's 90% done but hung up on dispute settlement won't survive ratification pressure.
  auto_industry: Congressman, if we sign the auto rules trilaterally *now*—75% RVC, labor inspections with real fines, phase-in period for suppliers—does that get you ratification momentum, or are Chapter 19 and dairy kill-switches for your members regardless?
  us_congress: Labor enforcement with real teeth—independent inspections, 20% tariff fines, 60-day correction windows—that's what my members need to see, and you've got it. Sign the auto package trilaterally *now* with those provisions locked in text; Chapter 19 and dairy we can negotiate in parallel, but I need to walk out of here with a credible labor enforcement win to hold the ratification line. Without that auto deal moving, Congress gets spooked that the whole thing collapses.
  labor_union: USTR, before we separate auto from Chapter 19, I need one thing clear: is the labor-enforcement mechanism — the independent inspections, the 20% tariff fines, the 60-day correction window — actually written into the auto rules text *right now*, or does it vanish if Chapter 19 and dairy don't close? Because if my members see labor enforcement as a hostage to those chapters, ratification dies.
  dairy_ag: Hold on—we're not parking dairy as a side conversation. Look, Canada signs the auto package trilaterally, we unlock dairy market access on a phased schedule tied to RVC implementation. That's the deal that moves Congress and gets us all to signature. Otherwise my members don't support ratification, and you're back to bilateral with Mexico.
  supply_chain_mfr: Look, the auto rules work—independent inspections, 20% fines, labor floor, 75% RVC, all trilateral. Congress just said they'll move ratification if that's signed. We can't let dairy and Chapter 19 kill a done deal. Sign the auto package this week, put a 90-day clock on the rest, and my supply chain stops holding investment hostage. Otherwise we're all frozen.
  auto_industry: Look, 75% RVC is workable *if* we get a real phase-in—18 months minimum for suppliers to retool, not overnight compliance. And the labor-value-content floor needs a clear definition: wages, benefits, headcount percentages—vague thresholds blow up our cost models and force re-sourcing we can't absorb. Give us those specifics in text this week, and we stop blocking trilateral signature.
